title: The Full Screen, Start To Finish
description: Thirty minutes played end to end with no commentary. Every answer from the series, in the order a real recruiter call runs, including the interruptions.

lines.text: Hi, is that Mingxia? It's Isabelle from the OpenAI Deployment Company. Can you hear me alright?
Hi Isabelle, yes, loud and clear. Thanks for making the time.
No problem at all. So, quick bit of context first. You applied through our Tomoro careers page back on the eleventh.
Tomoro is now part of the OpenAI Deployment Company. That went through at the start of July, so you'll see both names around.
I've been with the team since April, and I look after hiring across Australia. Sydney and Melbourne both.
That's helpful, thank you. I had seen the change, and I wasn't completely sure how the two boards related to each other.
Yeah, we're still tidying that up honestly. So, I've got half an hour.
I'd love to hear about your background, then talk about what the role actually is, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Nothing technical from me today. I'm not an engineer, so I'll be asking you to keep me with you.
That works. Say if I go too deep and I'll come back up.
Great. So do you want to start by telling me a bit about yourself?
Sure. I'm a software engineer, eight and a half years, almost all of it in regulated financial services at GBST.
We build capital-markets tax software for banks and super funds. So my customers have always been other institutions, not consumers.
Since April I've been running large language model systems in production. The main one handles security vulnerability management.
Every night a model drafts the day's remediation plans. Three different groups inside the business review and approve them the next morning.
Review time went from about forty-five minutes down to five, and the engineering hours we spend on it fell eighty percent.
It's now used by teams beyond the one I built it for.
Sorry, can I stop you there. Forty-five minutes down to five, per what?
Per item. Every week new security flaws get published against the open-source components our software is built from.
A regulated company has to prove it looked at every one of them. Most turn out not to matter in the way we actually run the software.
Working out which few genuinely matter used to take a person about forty-five minutes each. Now it's about five.
Got it. That's clearer, thank you. Carry on.
The reason I'm interested in this job is that the hard part of that project was never the model.
It was getting three groups with different incentives to trust it enough to act on it.
So I didn't switch anything over at the start. I ran it silently, next to the commercial tools the team already paid for, and compared.
When it agreed with them ninety-six percent of the time, and was also finding things they'd missed, people started acting on it.
So it replaced the commercial tools?
No, and that's deliberate. It runs alongside them and it stays advisory.
It flags something and a person makes the call. In a regulated environment that isn't a limitation, it's the design.
Interesting. And how much of that did you build yourself, versus a team?
That one I designed and built. It's since been picked up by other teams, which I didn't do, and I'm probably most pleased about that part.
On the older products at GBST I'd describe myself as a primary contributor rather than the author. I try to be precise about that.
You mentioned three groups reviewing it every morning. Who are they, in practice?
Image maintainers, application developers, and release managers. They want different things, which is the whole difficulty.
The maintainers want fewer changes. The developers want to ship. The release managers want a clean audit trail.
They all look at the same plan on one screen, and any of them can push back on it by talking to it before approving.
And they actually use it? People are usually good at ignoring internal tools.
They do now. They didn't at first, and that gap is the interesting part.
For weeks it ran and nobody acted on it. What changed was showing them it agreed with the tools they already believed in.
That's a good story. Keep that one for the engineers.
Let me tell you a bit about the role and then come back to you.
So we embed engineers directly inside customer organisations. Forward deployed engineering, that's the language we use.
You'd be on client sites a lot, sometimes up to three days a week, working with their teams to build and ship AI systems.
The Australian team is small and growing. We're across Sydney and Melbourne.
Can I ask something about that before we go on? I think there might be two versions of this role.
I applied through the Tomoro advert, which publishes a hundred and thirty to a hundred and eighty thousand.
Your own board has a Sydney forward deployed engineer role posted on the seventh of August at a hundred and thirty-five to three hundred and sixty, plus equity.
And the body of that one opens by saying you're seeking a senior applied AI software engineer. Which one am I being considered against?
Right, good question, and honestly a fair one. The Ashby posting is the current one. The Tomoro board is the legacy system.
Let me check where your application actually sits and come back to you on the level. It may well be the newer one.
Thank you, that's useful. I'd want to be considered against the forward deployed role if that's possible.
Noted. So tell me, what drew you to this? Is it the company, or is it the type of role?
Two reasons, and the first one is about me.
I've done the internal version of this job four or five times now, and the part I'm best at is the front half.
Sitting with the people who have the problem, arguing about what the system should refuse to do, and then building it.
At GBST the business analysis team were my internal customers for a set of agents I wrote for their workflow.
A report that used to take three days now runs in under thirty minutes.
And at Macquarie Business School I had to win an argument with a professor about a tutor that deliberately doesn't give students the answer.
That's client work with the invoice missing.
I like that. Say more about the tutor one.
It's running in a course now, about two hundred students. It reads each student's profile and that week's lecture material.
Then it walks them toward their own decision instead of handing over an answer. The easy build was the one that answers.
I had to make the case for the harder one, and win it, before I could build anything. That's the conversation I actually enjoy.
And the second reason?
Your own framing is the one I'd already arrived at. Your site describes the cycle as build, prove, generalise.
I built a platform called Foundry for that reason, because running agent crews showed me what was missing around them.
Every project rebuilds identity, audit, dispatch and cost accounting from scratch.
The model work is different every time. The plumbing underneath it isn't, and most teams pay for it again anyway.
And what's making you look right now? Is something not working where you are?
Nothing's wrong there. I led the AWS migration, and I've onboarded every engineer who's joined the core team since I took a lead role.
But the AI work is something I made space for, rather than something the company is organised around.
I want to be somewhere that's the product, and somewhere I see more than one industry a year.
Let me give you a picture of the team, since you'd be joining a small one.
Dan Edgar leads Australia. We launched here in December, so it's still early, and we're hiring across engineering and delivery.
Sydney and Melbourne got together for an offsite a couple of weeks ago, which was the first time everyone was in a room.
How big is the Australian team at the moment?
Smaller than the headline number you'll have read. That's part of the appeal, if it appeals.
It does. Being early enough that how things are done is still being decided is the part I'd want.
One thing I should check. This is hybrid, and there's a fair bit of client site work. Does that suit you?
It does. The part of the week I look forward to is the requirements conversation, not the implementation.
I built a design-phase agent at work whose whole job is running that conversation properly before anyone writes code.
I built a tool for the part of the job most engineers try to avoid, so I think the answer is yes.
Is there anything in the job description where you thought, that's not me?
Two things, and I'd rather name them than have you find them.
The first is that I've been running these systems in production for four months, since April. That's short and I know it.
Before that it was about seven months of retrieval and small-model work in my own projects.
What the four months bought me isn't model knowledge, it's the list of ways these systems fail quietly.
Meaning what, in practice?
My own retrieval pipeline ran for a month with every test passing and a silent quality regression inside it.
Nothing was red. Nothing alerted. The answers were just getting worse and no test could see it.
I only caught it because I'd built a check that verifies every quote against the source it came from.
You learn that once, in production, and then never design without it again.
That's a good answer. And the second thing?
Fine-tuning. Your advert lists it and I've deployed, not fine-tuned. Everything in production is hosted models through Bedrock.
What I have done is the decision next to it. Whether a problem needs a different model, better retrieval, or a harder verification step.
I'd expect to pick the tuning up. Knowing whether it's the right lever is the part that took me time.
That's fine, honestly. Most of our engineers aren't fine-tuning day to day.
One more from me. This is consulting. Have you worked that way before, on client engagements?
Not billably, no. All my client work has been through a product company, so I haven't lived the utilisation and timesheet side of it.
What I have done is scope work directly with a client. A tax relief capability for Qantas Super, the super fund.
We worked from the client's own reading of the twenty seventeen legislation rather than ours. And Macquarie commissioned a second phase after the first one shipped.
And team leadership? The role's pitched as a bit of a player-coach.
The coaching half I've done. Enablement and mentoring across the project group, and I led the AWS migration end to end.
I haven't carried an engineering-management title, so there's no reporting line on my record. I'd rather say that plainly.
One more, and this might be from the old advert. Have you used Spark?
No Spark. I've built batch data pipelines, Spring Batch on containers, doing corporate actions and parcel-level reconciliation.
So the shape of the problem is familiar, but I'd be learning the framework and I wouldn't pretend otherwise.
That's the legacy job description, I think. I'll check. It isn't on the current one.
Let me run through the boring bits quickly. Where are you based?
Sydney, out in Baulkham Hills.
And you're comfortable on client sites, up to three days a week?
Yes, comfortable with that.
There's some regional travel too, Singapore mostly. Is that alright?
That's fine. Can I ask roughly how often, so I know what I'd be agreeing to?
It varies by engagement, honestly. I'll find out what it's looked like for the Sydney team this year.
Notice period?
Four weeks.
And your right to work here?
Australian permanent resident. Full working rights, no sponsorship now or in the future.
Great. And what are you looking for, salary-wise?
Given what you said earlier about the Ashby posting being the current one, I'll answer against that band.
Based on the scope in that advert, owning architecture across engagements, setting the evaluation approach, mentoring.
I'd be looking at two hundred to two hundred and forty thousand base.
And I'd want to understand the equity component before fixing on a figure.
That's within range. It's not the bottom of it, but it's within range.
On equity, everyone gets a grant. I'd have to come back to you on the exact instrument.
That's fair. When you do, the three things I'd want to know are what instrument it is, how it vests, and what happens on a liquidity event.
I'm asking because it's a joint venture rather than an ordinary subsidiary, so I don't want to assume it works like a normal option grant.
That's a reasonable ask and not one I get often. I'll get you a proper answer.
Just so I set expectations, if it turns out your application sits on the legacy requisition, that band tops out lower.
Then I should be straight with you. A hundred and eighty is my floor, so I'd only be workable at the very top of that band.
I'd much rather be considered against the forward deployed role, if that's something you can do.
I think it will be. Leave that one with me.
We've got about five minutes. Do you have questions for me?
Three, if there's time. First, what does the rest of the process look like, and what's a normal timeline?
So after this there'd be a technical conversation with one of our engineers, and then a session with someone senior on the delivery side.
There's usually an exercise in there too. I'd need to confirm what the current one is, because we've changed it since the acquisition.
Timeline, usually two to three weeks end to end, assuming diaries cooperate.
That's helpful. Second one. I saw the Northslope announcement in July, that you'd agreed to acquire them.
Does that mean anything for the Australian team, or is it mostly a northern hemisphere thing?
Honestly, that's above my line. I know it's not closed yet. Let me ask and come back to you, because a few people have wondered.
No problem, and it's genuinely just curiosity. Last one, and this is the one I most want to know.
What does the Australian client work actually look like right now?
Is it mostly greenfield builds, or is a lot of it taking pilots that have stalled and getting them into production?
It's more of the second than people expect. A lot of our clients have done a proof of concept that never went anywhere.
The work is often as much about the organisation as the code. Getting people to actually use the thing.
That's the part I'd be most useful on, so that's good to hear.
The system I described earlier, the reason it worked wasn't the model. It was running it silently for weeks until people trusted it.
That's a good thing to say to the engineers, by the way. Say it exactly like that.
Alright, we're at time. This has been a really good conversation.
Thank you. Before we finish, what would the next step be, and roughly when should I expect to hear?
I'll write this up today and get it in front of the team this week. You should hear something by early next week.
And if I haven't heard by then, is it alright to email you directly?
Please do. I'll send you a note after this so you've got my address.
Perfect. And you'll come back to me on the requisition and the equity?
I will. Those two and the travel question. I've got them written down.
Thanks Isabelle, I appreciate you being straight about the two boards. Have a good afternoon.
You too. Speak soon.
